prompt: Same Thing, Two Descriptions.* A two-panel illustration on a white background. Left panel titled "Raw description": a small photo-style drawing of an ankle boot with a fine grid laid over it, and beside it a long scrolling column of numbers (e.g. "0, 1, 1, 0, 200, 232, 232 …") trailing off the bottom of the panel, labelled "784 brightness values". Right panel titled "Useful description": the same boot with three short labelled tags pointing at it: "tall shape", "heel at bottom-left", "closed top", and below it a short vector "[0.9, 0.1, 0.8, …]" labelled "a few meaningful numbers". A thin arrow between the panels labelled "representation learning". Flat educational style, muted colours, sans-serif labels. Takeaway: a representation replaces many meaningless numbers with fewer meaningful ones.

Encoder and Head.* A horizontal left-to-right flow diagram on a white background. Far left: a small grey 28×28 pixel image of a sneaker labelled "raw data (784 numbers)". Arrow into a tall blue trapezoid that narrows from left to right, labelled "ENCODER (early layers)". Out of its narrow end comes a short vertical stack of 6 coloured cells labelled "representation (e.g. 128 numbers)". Arrow into a small orange rectangle labelled "HEAD (e.g. one linear layer)". Arrow to a bar chart of 10 thin bars with the tallest labelled "Sneaker". Underneath the whole diagram, a long thin red arrow pointing right-to-left from the output back to the encoder, labelled "one loss, one backward pass: trains both parts together". Takeaway: the encoder builds the description, the head uses it, and both learn from the same error signal.

A Hierarchy of Features.* A four-column left-to-right diagram on a white background, with columns titled "Pixels", "Edges", "Parts", "Object". Column 1: a small greyscale ankle-boot image. Column 2: a 3×3 grid of tiny tiles, each showing a short line at a different angle (horizontal, vertical, diagonal) plus one small curve, labelled "layer 1: simple local patterns". Column 3: four slightly larger tiles showing a flat sole, a vertical shaft, a curved heel, and a rounded toe, labelled "layer 2–3: combinations of edges". Column 4: the boot outline assembled from those parts, labelled "later layers: whole objects". Thin grey arrows connect specific edge tiles to the parts they make up (e.g. the horizontal line and curve feed into "sole"). Along the bottom, a gradient bar from light to dark blue labelled "simple and local → complex and global". Takeaway: deep networks build complex features by combining simpler ones, layer by layer.

Three Routes to a Representation.* A diagram with one input on the left: a small greyscale Fashion-MNIST sneaker labelled "raw image". Three horizontal paths branch out to the right, each ending at the same small orange box labelled "same linear classifier". Top path: a person icon with a pencil, then a short list "ink, height, width, aspect…" labelled "handcrafted: 7 numbers". Middle path: a straight arrow with a long thin strip of grey cells labelled "raw pixels: 784 numbers". Bottom path: a blue trapezoid labelled "learned encoder (trained on other labelled data)", then a stack of coloured cells labelled "learned: 128 numbers". To the right of each orange box, a small accuracy badge: top "0.694", middle "0.803", bottom "0.868" (these are the measured results with 10,000 labels). Takeaway: the classifier is the same; only the description changes, and the description decides the result.

A CNN at a Glance.* A left-to-right pipeline diagram on a white background. Far left: a 28×28 greyscale sneaker image drawn as a flat square, labelled "input 1×28×28". Next: a stack of 16 thin, slightly offset translucent squares the same size, labelled "conv1 + ReLU → 16 feature maps (16×28×28)"; on the input image, a small highlighted 3×3 orange square with a dotted line to one pixel on the first feature map, labelled "one 3×3 filter, slid everywhere". Next: a smaller stack labelled "pool → 16×14×14". Next: a deeper stack of 32 smaller squares labelled "conv2 + ReLU → 32×14×14". Next: an even smaller stack labelled "pool → 32×7×7". Then a long thin vertical bar labelled "flatten → 1,568 numbers", then a small orange box labelled "head (fully connected)", then 10 thin output bars with the tallest labelled "Sneaker". Above the first half, a bracket labelled "ENCODER: finds patterns, keeps the 2D layout"; above the second half, a bracket labelled "HEAD: makes the decision". Takeaway: a CNN is an encoder made of local, shared filters followed by a small classifier.

Growing Receptive Fields.* Three stacked square grids drawn in perspective, bottom to top, on a white background. Bottom grid: a 12×12 pixel grid labelled "input image", with a faint sneaker outline drawn across it. Middle grid: a smaller grid labelled "layer 1 feature map". Top grid: a still smaller grid labelled "layer 2 feature map". One single highlighted cell on the top grid (orange) has lines fanning down to a 3×3 orange block on the middle grid, and from the edges of that block, lines fan further down to a larger highlighted block on the input grid (light orange, about 8×8 cells), which covers the toe of the sneaker. Labels on the side: "3×3 window", "covers 8×8 pixels". Takeaway: each layer looks at a small window of the layer below, so deeper units see more of the image.

What Each Part of a CNN Contributes.* A horizontal band divided into five labelled panels connected by arrows, white background. Panel 1 "Tensor (N, C, H, W)": a small stack of greyscale squares with the axes N, C, H, W marked. Panel 2 "Convolution": a 3×3 orange filter sliding over a grid with a curved arrow, beside it the words "local + shared weights". Panel 3 "Feature maps": three small maps showing a vertical edge, a horizontal edge and a filled silhouette of a boot, in red/blue. Panel 4 "Pooling": a 4×4 grid with coloured 2×2 blocks shrinking to a 2×2 grid, labelled "smaller maps, larger receptive field". Panel 5 "Head": a flatten bar into a small orange box, then a bar chart with "Ankle boot" tallest. Beneath panels 2–4 a bracket labelled "repeat: edges → parts → shapes". Takeaway: each component has one job, and together they turn pixels into a decision while respecting the image's 2D structure.

From Text to Embeddings.* A vertical flow of five labelled rows on a white background, connected by downward arrows. Row 1 "Raw text": a speech-bubble containing `This movie wasn't GOOD.
It was great!`. Row 2 "Tokens": seven rounded rectangles in a line: `this` `movie` `wasn't` `good` `it` `was` `great`. Row 3 "Token IDs": the same seven boxes now showing integers `11` `17` `291` `49` `9` `13` `80`, with a small inset table on the right labelled "vocabulary" listing "2 → the", "11 → this", "49 → good", "80 → great". Row 4 "Embeddings": below each ID box, a short vertical column of 6 coloured cells (heat-map colours), labelled "one learned vector per token". Row 5 "Model": the columns feed into a single orange box labelled "network", with an output arrow to a badge "positive". Takeaway: text becomes numbers in two steps, first IDs (arbitrary labels), then embeddings (meaningful vectors).

An Embedding Is a Lookup Table.* On the left, a tall narrow table drawn as a grid with 8 columns and many rows (only some drawn, with "⋮" between groups), with row labels on its left edge: "0 <pad>", "1 <unk>", "2 the", "⋮", "49 good", "⋮", "80 great", "⋮", "10001 …". The rows for "good" and "great" are highlighted in orange and blue. On the right, a token-ID box "49" with an arrow pointing into the table at row 49, and a second arrow coming out to the right holding the 8-number orange row, labelled "vector for 'good'". Beneath the table, a caption box: "Same result as one-hot × table, without multiplying by 10,001 zeros". Along the top, a bracket over the table's columns labelled "embedding_dim = 8", and along the left a bracket labelled "num_embeddings = 10,002". Takeaway: an embedding layer stores one learnable vector per token and simply looks it up.

Cosine Similarity Is About Angle.* Four small square panels in a row on a white background, each showing x and y axes and two arrows from the origin. Panel 1 "same direction, cos = 1.000": a short blue arrow [1,1] lying along a longer orange arrow [2,2]. Panel 2 "45°, cos = 0.707": blue [1,0] along the x-axis and orange [1,1] at 45°, with the angle marked. Panel 3 "right angle, cos = 0.000": blue [1,0] and orange [0,1], with a small square marking the right angle. Panel 4 "opposite, cos = −1.000": blue [1,1] and orange [−1,−1] pointing away from each other. Beneath all panels: "Length doesn't matter; only the angle does." Takeaway: cosine similarity measures whether two vectors point the same way.

Static vs. Contextual.* Two side-by-side panels on a white background. Left panel titled "Static embedding": the two sentences "sat by the river bank" and "cash at the bank" each written on a line, with the word "bank" in both connected by arrows to one single shared vector (a column of 6 grey cells) in the middle, labelled "one vector for every use of 'bank'". Right panel titled "Contextual representation": the same two sentences, but now each "bank" has its own vector: the first a column of blue-green cells with a small river icon, the second a column of gold cells with a coin icon, and thin arrows from "river" and "cash" bending into their respective vectors, labelled "vector depends on the neighbours". Takeaway: static embeddings give a word one meaning; contextual models give it a meaning per sentence.

One Table, Two Objectives.* A diagram with a single grey grid on the left labelled "embedding table (random at start)". Two arrows branch right. Upper arrow labelled "trained to predict sentiment (labels)" leads to a 2D scatter where green positive words (excellent, superb, great) sit far left, red negative words (awful, worst, dull) sit far right, and blue family words (husband, wife, mother) and purple music words (music, jazz, score) are scattered randomly in between; caption "one strong axis: positive ↔ negative". Lower arrow labelled "trained to predict neighbouring words (no labels)" leads to a scatter with four tidy separate clusters (green, red, blue, purple); caption "clusters by topic and usage". Takeaway: what an embedding learns is decided by its training objective.

An RNN Unrolled Over Time.* A horizontal diagram on a white background with three identical blue rounded boxes in a row, each labelled "RNN cell (same weights)". Below each box, an upward arrow from a word token: "dog", "bites", "man", labelled x₁, x₂, x₃. Between the boxes, rightward orange arrows labelled h₁ and h₂, and a final orange arrow leaving the third box labelled h₃ "final hidden state: a summary of the whole sentence". On the far left, a small grey circle feeding the first box labelled "h₀ = zeros". Above the diagram, a curved bracket spanning all three boxes labelled "one cell, applied once per step". Takeaway: an RNN reads in order, passing its memory forward from step to step.

The LSTM's Memory Lane.* A single wide LSTM cell drawn as a rounded rectangle on a white background. Across the top runs a thick straight horizontal green line labelled "cell state (long-term memory)", entering on the left as c(t−1) and leaving on the right as c(t). On this line sit two small circles: a "×" circle fed from below by a small gate box labelled "forget gate f (0–1)", and a "+" circle fed from below by a box labelled "input gate × new candidate". Lower in the cell, a thinner orange line carries the hidden state h(t−1) in from the left and h(t) out on the right, with a box labelled "output gate" connecting the cell state down to h(t). The current input x(t) enters from the bottom and feeds all three gate boxes. A callout beside the green line: "if f ≈ 1, memory and gradient flow straight through". Takeaway: the LSTM keeps a protected memory line that gates can preserve across many steps.

Chain vs. Direct Access.* Two horizontal panels on a white background, each with the same six word boxes in a row: "The", "film", "…", "…", "director", "was". Top panel titled "RNN: information travels along a chain": orange arrows link each box to the next, left to right, and a long faint red arrow underneath points from "was" back to "film", labelled "signal must pass through every step in between". Bottom panel titled "Attention: every word can look at every word": from "was", six curved blue lines of different thickness fan out to all six boxes, with the line to "film" drawn thickest and labelled "high weight", and the lines to "…" thin, labelled "low weight". Caption beneath the bottom panel: "distance doesn't matter; relevance does". Takeaway: attention replaces a long chain of steps with direct, weighted connections.

The Road to Attention.* A left-to-right timeline of four stepping-stone panels on a white background, connected by arrows. Panel 1 "Bag of words / averaging": a jumbled pile of word tiles, caption "order-blind". Panel 2 "RNN": a chain of three blue boxes passing an orange memory arrow, caption "order-aware, but memory fades". Panel 3 "LSTM": the chain with a green protected memory line on top and small gate symbols, caption "gates can keep memory, but one-at-a-time and through a fixed-size state". Panel 4 "Attention": six word boxes with blue curved lines connecting each to all others, caption "direct, parallel, contextual". Beneath the timeline, an arrow labelled "→ Transformers (Module 6)". Takeaway: each step fixed the previous step's main limitation, leading to attention.

Two Separate Spaces vs. One Shared Space.* Two panels on a white background. Left panel titled "Separate encoders, separate spaces": two unconnected circles. The left circle, labelled "image space", contains small greyscale thumbnails of a bag, a sneaker and a dress scattered around. The right circle, labelled "text space", contains the phrases "a bag", "a sneaker", "a dress" scattered in different positions, with a large red "≠" between the circles and a note "no way to compare". Right panel titled "Shared space": one large circle with three clusters; each cluster pairs a thumbnail with its phrase side by side (bag thumbnail next to "a bag", sneaker next to "a sneaker", dress next to "a dress"), with short green lines linking each pair. Takeaway: a shared space puts matching images and text close together, so they can be compared directly.

The Contrastive Similarity Matrix.* A 4×4 grid on a white background. Along the left edge, four small greyscale thumbnails labelled image 1 to 4 (a bag, a sneaker, a dress, a coat). Along the top, four caption boxes labelled caption 1 to 4 ("a photo of a bag", "a picture of a sneaker", "an image showing a dress", "a coat on a plain background"). The four diagonal cells are coloured bright green with an upward arrow and the label "pull together (positive pairs)". All twelve off-diagonal cells are coloured pale red with a downward arrow, labelled "push apart (negative pairs)". On the right, a bracket around one row labelled "row: which caption fits this image?"; on the bottom, a bracket around one column labelled "column: which image fits this caption?". Takeaway: contrastive learning makes the diagonal of the similarity matrix high and everything else low.

How CLIP Is Trained and Used.* Two panels on a white background. Left panel titled "Training": a column of four varied photo thumbnails (a dog on a beach, a bowl of noodles, a city skyline, a guitar) flowing into a blue box "image encoder", and a column of four matching caption snippets ("my dog loves the beach", "homemade ramen", "skyline at dusk", "vintage guitar for sale") flowing into a purple box "text encoder". Both boxes feed a 4×4 grid with a bright green diagonal labelled "contrastive loss". Right panel titled "Zero-shot classification": a new photo of a cat flows into the image encoder; a list of written labels "a photo of a dog", "a photo of a cat", "a photo of a car" flows into the text encoder; arrows lead to three similarity bars, with the "cat" bar tallest and highlighted. Takeaway: CLIP learns a shared space from image–text pairs, then classifies new images by comparing them with text descriptions.

Shared-Space Recipe.* A symmetric diagram on a white background. On the left, a stack of greyscale clothing thumbnails flows into a blue trapezoid "image encoder (CNN)", then a small blue box "projection → 32 numbers, length 1". On the right, a stack of captions flows into a purple trapezoid "text encoder (embeddings)", then a small purple box "projection → 32 numbers, length 1". Both projections point into a central circle labelled "shared space", drawn with ten small coloured clusters, each with a few dots (images) and a star (text) side by side. Below the circle, a small 4×4 matrix with a green diagonal labelled "contrastive loss: pull matches together, push others apart". Beneath everything, three small output icons with arrows from the circle: a magnifying glass "search", a tag "classify by description", and a pair of linked images "find similar". Takeaway: two encoders plus projections plus contrastive training produce one space where images and text can be compared.

How to Read a 2D Picture of a Representation.* A three-column comparison card on a white background. Column 1, "Full representation (64 numbers)": a small cube filled with coloured point clouds, labelled "the truth: measure here". Column 2, "PCA (a shadow)": a light source casting the cube's shadow onto a wall, producing overlapping coloured blobs; a tag below reads "keeps: big directions of spread · loses: many neighbourhoods". Column 3, "t-SNE (a rearrangement)": the same coloured clouds pulled apart into neat separate islands on a flat sheet, with dashed arrows showing islands that could be swapped in position; a tag below reads "keeps: who is next to whom · loses: distances between islands". Under all three columns, a banner: "Pictures illustrate; numbers decide." Takeaway: both methods distort in different ways, so always back a 2D picture with a measurement in the full space.

Module 5 at a Glance.* A single summary poster on a white background, arranged as a central hub with five spokes. Centre: a circle labelled "Learned representation: a compact, task-shaped description of raw data". Spoke 1 (top-left) "Images → CNN": a small filter sliding over a clothing thumbnail, caption "local, shared filters; edges → parts → objects". Spoke 2 (top-right) "Text → embeddings": a word token turning into a short coloured vector, caption "meaning shaped by the training objective". Spoke 3 (right) "Sequences → RNN → attention": a short chain of boxes fading out, then a fan of direct connections, caption "from step-by-step memory to direct access". Spoke 4 (bottom-right) "Images + text → shared space": a thumbnail and a caption meeting at the same point, caption "contrastive learning". Spoke 5 (bottom-left) "Evaluating representations": a small bar chart and a scatter plot with a magnifying glass, caption "probes, neighbours, sign tests; pictures only illustrate". A small arrow from the hub to the bottom edge labelled "Next: Transformers (Module 6)". Takeaway: every part of Module 5 is a way of learning, or measuring, a better description of raw data.

The Transformer at a Glance.* A vertical stack diagram on a white background, read bottom to top. At the bottom, a row of six character tiles "F", "i", "r", "s", "t", " " labelled "input tokens". Above each tile, a small grey vector bar labelled "token embedding", plus a small striped bar beside it labelled "+ position embedding". Above that, a large rounded rectangle labelled "Transformer block × 3", drawn as a slightly 3D stack of three identical cards. Inside the front card, two stacked sub-boxes: a blue box "attention: tokens exchange information" with criss-crossing thin lines between six small circles, and an orange box "feed-forward: each token thinks on its own" with six separate small arrows. Above the stack, a thin grey box "final layer norm", then a green box "output head", then at the top six small bar charts (one above each position), each with one tallest bar, labelled "next-token predictions (65 scores each)". Takeaway: a Transformer turns a sequence of tokens into a sequence of predictions through embeddings, a stack of blocks and an output head.

The Residual Stream.* A diagram on a white background showing two vertical lanes side by side, labelled at the bottom "good lord" and "evil lord", each starting from a tile with the character "d". Each lane is a thick vertical arrow (the stream) rising through three horizontal dashed lines labelled "block 1", "block 2", "block 3". At each block, a small side-box with a "+" feeds into the stream: the left lane's boxes are tinted green and labelled "context from 'good'", the right lane's tinted red and labelled "context from 'evil'". The two lanes start the same colour (grey) at the bottom and gradually take on green and red tints as they rise. At the top, a small badge between the lanes reads "same token, different meaning". Takeaway: each block adds context to a token's vector, so identical tokens in different contexts drift apart.

Module 6 Roadmap.* A horizontal roadmap on a white background built on the Transformer stack from IMAGE 6.1.1, drawn small on the left. Five numbered signposts point to parts of it: "6.2 Inputs: tokens, IDs, embeddings, positions" pointing at the bottom; "6.3 Attention: queries, keys, values, masks, heads" pointing at the blue attention box; "6.4 The block: feed-forward, residuals, layer norm" pointing at the whole block card; "6.5 The full model: decoder-only, output head" pointing at the top; "6.6 Training and generation" pointing at a small text page emerging from the top. Takeaway: each remaining note of Module 6 opens up one part of the system you have just seen working.

From Text File to Training Batch.* A left-to-right pipeline on a white background with six labelled stages joined by arrows. Stage 1 "split": a long horizontal bar representing the file, coloured blue for the first 90% ("train") and orange for the last 10% ("validation"). Stage 2 "tokenise": the phrase "To be, or" shown split into tiles "T" "o" " " "b" "e" "," " " "o" "r". Stage 3 "encode": the same tiles now showing numbers "32 53 1 40 43 6 1 53 56". Stage 4 "window": a long strip of numbers with a highlighted bracket of 64 cells labelled "context = 64". Stage 5 "shift": two stacked strips, the upper labelled "x (input)" and the lower labelled "y (target)", with the lower one offset by one cell to the left and diagonal arrows linking each x cell to the y cell above-right. Stage 6 "batch": a stack of 32 such strips forming a block labelled "(32, 64)". Takeaway: text becomes training batches through splitting, tokenising, encoding, windowing and shifting.

Three Ways to Tokenise the Same Line.* Three horizontal rows on a white background, each showing the phrase "Thou art a villain" broken into coloured tiles. Row 1, labelled "characters (vocab 65)": eighteen small tiles, one per character including spaces. Row 2, labelled "words (vocab 12,571)": seven tiles "Thou" " " "art" " " "a" " " "villain". Row 3, labelled "BPE, 200 merges (vocab 265)": ten tiles "Th" "ou" " " "art" " " "a" " " "v" "ill" "ain". To the right of each row, a small bar showing its length in tokens. Beneath, a caption: "Bigger vocabulary → fewer tokens → more text per context window, but a bigger embedding table and more unknown words." Takeaway: tokenisation trades vocabulary size against sequence length.

Attention as Focused Reading.* The sentence "The animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired" written in a single row of word tiles on a white background. From the tile "it", curved blue lines arc to every earlier word, with line thickness showing attention weight: a very thick line to "animal", a thin line to "street", and hair-thin lines to the rest. A small callout under "it" reads "new vector for 'it' = mostly 'animal' + a little of the others". In a faint second row underneath, the same sentence ending "...too wide" shows the thick line going to "street" instead. Takeaway: attention lets each word pull in information from the words most relevant to it, and relevance depends on context.

Self-Attention, Step by Step.* A left-to-right flow on a white background. Left: a column of four token tiles "the", "cat", "sat", "down", each with a short grey vector. Each vector splits through three small coloured boxes "W_Q", "W_K", "W_V" into three coloured vectors: query (purple), key (green), value (orange). Middle: a 4×4 grid labelled "scores = Q·Kᵀ", built from purple rows meeting green columns, with one cell highlighted and the label "q_sat · k_cat". Then an arrow labelled "÷ √d, mask, softmax" leads to a second 4×4 grid in shades of blue labelled "weights (each row sums to 1)". Right: the weight grid multiplies a stack of four orange value vectors, producing four new vectors labelled "outputs: one context-aware vector per token". Takeaway: attention is compare (Q·K), normalise (softmax), then average (weights × V).

Inside a Multi-Head Attention Layer.* A vertical diagram on a white background. At the bottom, an input tensor drawn as a block labelled "(B, T, 64)". It enters a box "one linear layer → Q, K, V". Three thin arrows lead into four parallel narrow columns labelled "head 1" to "head 4", each showing a small purple Q, green K and orange V block of width 16, a small lower-triangular blue grid labelled "softmax(QKᵀ/√16 + mask)", and an output block. The four head outputs join side by side into a single block labelled "concatenate → (B, T, 64)", then pass through a box labelled "output projection", producing "(B, T, 64)" at the top. A side note at the right of the heads: "each head can learn a different relationship". Takeaway: multi-head attention runs several small attention operations in parallel and recombines their results.

Anatomy of a Transformer Block.* A vertical diagram on a white background, read bottom to top. A thick grey vertical arrow, labelled "residual stream x", runs straight up the full height on the left. Two branches leave it to the right and rejoin it. Lower branch: a thin grey box "LayerNorm", then a blue box "multi-head self-attention (tokens exchange information)", then an arrow back into a "+" circle on the main stream. Upper branch: a thin grey box "LayerNorm", then an orange box "feed-forward network (each token on its own)", then an arrow back into a second "+" circle. Small labels on the branches read "sub-layer 1" and "sub-layer 2". At the bottom and top, the shape "(B, T, 64)" is written, unchanged. Takeaway: a block is two branches, attention and feed-forward, each normalised on the way in and added back to the main stream.

Post-Norm vs. Pre-Norm.* Two side-by-side vertical block diagrams on a white background. Left, titled "Post-norm (original)": the main stream goes up into a "+" that combines it with the output of a blue "attention" box, and then passes **through** a grey "LayerNorm" box sitting on the main stream itself, before the same pattern repeats with an orange "feed-forward" box. The LayerNorm boxes are drawn across the main path, with a small red note "every gradient must pass through the norms". Right, titled "Pre-norm (modern)": the main stream is an unbroken straight grey arrow from bottom to top; LayerNorm boxes sit only on the side branches, before the attention and feed-forward boxes, and the branches rejoin through "+" circles. A small green note reads "clean residual highway". Takeaway: pre-norm keeps the residual path free of normalisation, which makes deep stacks easier to train.

Four Ingredients, Four Jobs.* A 2×2 grid of illustrated cards on a white background. Card 1, "Attention": several small circles (tokens) connected by curved lines of varying thickness, caption "gather: tokens exchange information". Card 2, "Feed-forward": a single token vector expanding into a wide layer and contracting again, caption "process: each token thinks on its own". Card 3, "Residual connection": a straight highway arrow with a side road merging back via a "+", caption "preserve: add changes, keep the original; gradients flow straight through". Card 4, "Layer norm": three bars of very different heights being resized to the same height, caption "stabilise: every token at a standard scale". Takeaway: each ingredient of the block does a distinct job, and the block needs all four.

Our Decoder-Only Language Model.* A vertical architecture diagram on a white background, read bottom to top. Bottom: a row of character tiles "t", ",", " ", "f", "o", "r" labelled "token IDs (B, 64)". Above: two side-by-side boxes, "token embedding 65 × 64" and "position embedding 64 × 64", joined by a "+" into a bar labelled "(B, 64, 64)". Above that: three stacked identical cards labelled "pre-norm Transformer block", each showing a small "LN → causal attention → +" and "LN → FFN → +". Above: a thin box "final LayerNorm", then a green box "output head 64 → 65", then a bar labelled "logits (B, 64, 65)". At the very top, two branches: left, "softmax → next-character probabilities" with a small bar chart; right, "cross-entropy with targets → loss". Side labels: "162,561 parameters". Takeaway: the language model is embeddings, three blocks, a final norm and a head.

Inside an Encoder–Decoder Block.* Two vertical stacks side by side on a white background. Left stack, labelled "encoder (reads the source)": a row of source tokens "the" "cat" "sat" at the bottom, rising through a block with "self-attention (no mask)" and "feed-forward", producing a row of green output vectors at the top. Right stack, labelled "decoder (writes the target)": target tokens "<start>" "le" "chat" at the bottom, rising through a block with three sub-layers: "causal self-attention", then "cross-attention", then "feed-forward". From the cross-attention box, a bundle of arrows reaches across to the encoder's green output vectors, labelled "keys and values from the encoder"; a small purple arrow inside the decoder is labelled "queries from the decoder". Takeaway: cross-attention lets each output token consult the whole input sequence.

Learning vs. Generating.* Two horizontal panels on a white background. Top panel, titled "Training (teacher forcing, all positions at once)": a row of real character tiles "R O M E O :" feeding upward into a wide blue box "Transformer", which outputs a row of predicted tiles above every position; each prediction is compared, via a small "≠ / =" symbol, with the true next character shown in a green row ("O M E O : \n"), and all comparisons feed into one red box "loss → backpropagation". Bottom panel, titled "Generation (one character at a time)": the prompt "ROMEO:\n" feeds into the same blue box, which outputs one distribution bar chart at the last position only; an arrow labelled "sample" picks a character "T", which loops back with a curved arrow to the end of the input row; small numbers 1, 2, 3 on successive loops show "Th", "Tho"... Takeaway: training checks every position against real text in one pass; generation builds text one choice at a time from the model's own output.

Module 6 in One Picture.* A circular cycle diagram on a white background with five stations connected by arrows. Station 1 "Text → tokens → windows" (a page icon turning into tiles and a bracket of 64). Station 2 "Transformer" (a small stack of three blocks with attention lines). Station 3 "Loss" (a bar chart with the true next character highlighted, labelled "−log p(correct)"). Station 4 "Update" (a downhill arrow on a curve, labelled "AdamW, warmup, cosine, clipping"). From Station 2 a second branch leaves the cycle to Station 5 "Generate" (a chain of characters growing one tile at a time, with a small dial labelled "temperature / top-k / top-p"). In the centre: "next-token prediction". Takeaway: the same model learns by predicting the next token on real text, and writes by predicting the next token on its own output.
